title: Real-World Fault Detection for C-Extended Python Projects with Automated Unit Test Generation
comment: Accepted at the 19th IEEE International Conference on Software Testing, Verification and Validation (ICST) 2026, Daejeon, Republic of Korea
summary: Many popular Python libraries use C-extensions for performance-critical operations allowing users to combine the best of the two worlds: The simplicity and versatility of Python and the performance of C. A drawback of this approach is that exceptions raised in C can bypass Python's exception handling and cause the entire interpreter to crash. These crashes are real faults if they occur when calling a public API. While automated test generation should, in principle, detect such faults, crashes in native code can halt the test process entirely, preventing detection or reproduction of the underlying errors and inhibiting coverage of non-crashing parts of the code. To overcome this problem, we propose separating the generation and execution stages of the test-generation process. We therefore adapt Pynguin, an automated test case generation tool for Python, to use subprocess-execution. Executing each generated test in an isolated subprocess prevents a crash from halting the test generation process itself. This allows us to (1) detect such faults, (2) generate reproducible crash-revealing test cases for them, (3) allow studying the underlying faults, and (4) enable test generation for non-crashing parts of the code. To evaluate our approach, we created a dataset consisting of 1648 modules from 21 popular Python libraries with C-extensions. Subprocess-execution allowed automated testing of up to 56.5% more modules and discovered 213 unique crash causes, revealing 32 previously unknown faults.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using subprocess-execution in automated testing to isolate and detect crashes caused by C-extensions in Python libraries, enabling robust fault detection and improved test coverage.
AI.motivation: C-extensions in Python libraries can cause interpreter crashes when exceptions in C code bypass Python's exception handling; these crashes hinder automated testing and fault reproduction.
AI.method: The authors modify Pynguin, an automated test generation tool, to execute each generated test in an isolated subprocess, preventing crashes from halting the overall test process.
AI.result: Subprocess-execution enabled testing of up to 56.5% more modules across 21 popular Python libraries and uncovered 213 unique crash causes, including 32 previously unknown faults.
AI.conclusion: Isolating test execution in subprocesses effectively mitigates the impact of native code crashes, enabling reliable fault detection, reproducible test cases, and broader test coverage for Python libraries with C-extensions.

title: A LINDDUN-based Privacy Threat Modeling Framework for GenAI
summary: As generative AI (GenAI) systems become increasingly prevalent across various technological stacks, the question of how such systems handle sensitive and personal data flows becomes increasingly important. Specifically, both the ability to harness and process large swaths of information as well as their stochastic nature raise key concerns related to both security and privacy. Unfortunately, while some of the traditional security threat modeling can effectively identify certain violations, privacy-related issues are often overlooked. To respond to these challenges, we introduce a novel domain-specific privacy threat modeling framework to support the privacy threat analysis of GenAI-based applications. This framework is constructed through a two-pronged approach: (1) a systematic review of the emerging literature on GenAI privacy threats, and (2) a case-driven application to a representative Chatbot system. These efforts yield a foundational GenAI privacy threat modeling framework built on LINDDUN. The new framework affects three out of the seven privacy threat types of LINDDUN and introduces 100 new GenAI examples to the knowledge base. Its effectiveness is validated on an AI Agent system, which demonstrates that a comprehensive privacy analysis can be supported by the new framework.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel domain-specific privacy threat modeling framework for generative AI (GenAI) systems, extending the LINDDUN methodology with 100 new GenAI-specific examples and validating its effectiveness on an AI Agent system.
AI.motivation: Traditional security threat modeling often overlooks privacy issues in GenAI systems, despite their extensive data processing and stochastic behavior, necessitating a specialized privacy-focused framework.
AI.method: The authors采用 a two-pronged approach: (1) a systematic literature review on GenAI privacy threats, and (2) a case study applying the framework to a representative chatbot system, extending the LINDDUN model.
AI.result: The framework extends LINDDUN by impacting three of its seven privacy threat types and incorporates 100 new GenAI-specific threat examples; it was validated on an AI Agent system, enabling comprehensive privacy analysis.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively supports privacy threat analysis in GenAI applications, addressing gaps in existing methodologies and enhancing privacy assurance in generative AI systems.

title: Can Adjusting Hyperparameters Lead to Green Deep Learning: An Empirical Study on Correlations between Hyperparameters and Energy Consumption of Deep Learning Models
summary: Context: Along with developing Deep learning (DL) models, larger datasets and more complex model structures are applied, leading to rising computing resources and energy consumption, which is an alert that green DL models should receive more attention. Objective: This paper focuses on a novel view to analyze DL energy consumption: the effect of hyperparameters on the energy cost of DL models. Method: Our approach involves using mutation operators to simulate how practitioners adjust hyperparameters, such as epochs and learning rates. We train the original and mutated models separately and gather energy information and run-time performance metrics. Moreover, we focus on the parallel scenario where multiple DL models are trained in parallel. Results: To examine the effect of hyperparameters on energy consumption, we conducted extensive experiments on five real-world DL models. The results show that (1) many hyperparameters studied have a (positive or negative) correlation with energy consumption, (2) adjusting hyperparameters can make DL models greener, i.e., lead to less energy consumption without performance damage, and (3) in a parallel environment, energy consumption becomes more susceptible to change. Conclusions: We suggest that hyperparameters need more attention in developing DL models, as appropriately adjusting hyperparameters would cause green DL models.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the impact of hyperparameters on the energy consumption of deep learning models, proposing the use of mutation operators to analyze changes in energy cost and performance; experiments show that hyperparameter tuning can reduce energy usage without sacrificing performance, especially in parallel training setups.
AI.motivation: The increasing energy consumption of deep learning models due to larger datasets and complex architectures calls for greener solutions; this work highlights hyperparameter tuning as a critical yet underexplored factor affecting energy efficiency.
AI.method: The authors apply mutation operators to simulate hyperparameter changes (e.g., epochs, learning rate), train both original and mutated models, and measure energy consumption and performance; they also evaluate these effects in parallel training environments.
AI.result: Experiments across five real-world DL models show that hyperparameters are significantly correlated with energy consumption, proper tuning can reduce energy use without degrading performance, and energy consumption is more sensitive in parallel training scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Hyperparameter selection significantly influences energy efficiency in deep learning, and mindful tuning can lead to greener models, suggesting the need to prioritize hyperparameter optimization in sustainable AI development.

title: PQC-LEO: An Evaluation Framework for Post-Quantum Cryptographic Algorithms
summary: Advances in quantum computing threaten digital communication security by undermining the foundations of current public-key cryptography through Shor's quantum algorithm. This has driven the development of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), a new set of algorithms resistant to quantum attacks. While NIST has standardised several PQC schemes, challenges remain in their adoption. This paper introduces the PQC-LEO framework, a benchmarking suite designed to automate the evaluation of PQC computational and networking performance across x86 and ARM architectures. A proof-of-concept evaluation was conducted to demonstrate the framework's capabilities and highlight its application in supporting ongoing research on the adoption of PQC algorithms. The results show that there is a greater performance reduction in implementing PQC methods with higher security on ARM architectures than on the x86 architecture.

AI.tldr: This paper presents PQC-LEO, a framework for automated benchmarking of post-quantum cryptography on x86 and ARM systems, showing that ARM platforms suffer more significant performance hits under high-security PQC, highlighting challenges for widespread adoption.
AI.motivation: The threat posed by quantum computing to current public-key cryptography via Shor's algorithm necessitates the transition to post-quantum cryptography. However, adoption challenges, particularly performance on different hardware platforms, require systematic evaluation tools.
AI.method: The authors designed and implemented PQC-LEO, a benchmarking framework that automates the evaluation of computational and networking performance of post-quantum cryptography algorithms on x86 and ARM architectures. They conducted a proof-of-concept evaluation using standardized PQC schemes to assess performance differences.
AI.result: The evaluation showed that PQC implementations incur greater performance degradation on ARM architectures compared to x86, especially as security levels increase, indicating potential bottlenecks for deploying PQC in embedded and low-power systems.
AI.conclusion: The PQC-LEO framework effectively automates the benchmarking of post-quantum cryptography algorithms across different architectures, revealing notably higher performance overhead on ARM compared to x86, particularly under higher security requirements, which has implications for PQC adoption in resource-constrained environments.

title: Story Point Estimation Using Large Language Models
summary: This study investigates the use of large language models (LLMs) for story point estimation. Story points are unitless, project-specific effort estimates that help developers on the scrum team forecast which product backlog items they plan to complete in a sprint. To facilitate this process, machine learning models, especially deep neural networks, have been applied to predict the story points based on the title and description of each item. However, such machine learning models require sufficient amounts of training data (with ground truth story points annotated by human developers) from the same software project to achieve decent prediction performance. This motivated us to explore whether LLMs are capable of (RQ1) predicting story points without training data or (RQ2) with only a few training data points. Our empirical results with four LLMs on 16 software projects show that, without any training data (zero-shot prompting), LLMs can predict story points better than supervised deep learning models trained on 80% of the data. The prediction performance of LLMs can be further improved with a few training examples (few-shot prompting). In addition, a recent study explored the use of comparative judgments (between a given pair of items which one requires more effort to implement) instead of directly annotating the story points to reduce the cognitive burden on developers. Therefore, this study also explores (RQ3) whether comparative judgments are easier to predict than story points for LLMs and (RQ4) whether comparative judgments can serve as few-shot examples for LLMs to improve their predictions of story points. Empirical results suggest that it is not easier for LLMs to predict comparative judgments than to directly estimate the story points, but comparative judgments can serve as few-shot examples to improve the LLMs' prediction performance as well as the human-annotated story points.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates large language models (LLMs) for story point estimation in agile development, showing that LLMs outperform supervised deep learning models in zero-shot settings and improve further with few-shot prompting, including using comparative judgments as context.
AI.motivation: Traditional machine learning models for story point estimation require large amounts of labeled project-specific data, which is often scarce. This limitation motivates the exploration of LLMs that can predict story points with little or no training data, reducing dependency on annotated datasets.
AI.method: The authors evaluate four LLMs across 16 software projects using zero-shot and few-shot prompting to predict story points. They also investigate whether comparative judgments (effort comparisons between task pairs) are easier to predict than absolute story points and whether such judgments can improve story point predictions when used as few-shot examples.
AI.result: LLMs outperform supervised deep learning models trained on 80% of labeled data in zero-shot story point prediction. Performance improves with few-shot examples. Comparative judgments are not easier for LLMs to predict than story points, but they are effective as few-shot prompts to enhance story point estimation accuracy.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are a promising alternative for story point estimation in data-scarce settings, achieving strong performance without project-specific training data. Comparative judgments, while not simpler to predict, can effectively support few-shot learning for improved estimation.

title: Alkaid: Resilience to Edit Errors in Provably Secure Steganography via Distance-Constrained Encoding
summary: While provably secure steganography provides strong concealment by ensuring stego carriers are indistinguishable from natural samples, such systems remain vulnerable to real-world edit errors (e.g., insertions, deletions, substitutions) because their decoding depends on perfect synchronization and lacks error-correcting capability. To bridge this gap, we propose Alkaid, a provably secure steganographic scheme resilient to edit errors via distance-constrained encoding. The key innovation integrates the minimum distance decoding principle directly into the encoding process by enforcing a strict lower bound on the edit distance between codewords of different messages. Specifically, if two candidate codewords violate this bound, they are merged to represent the same message, thereby guaranteeing reliable recovery. While maintaining provable security, we theoretically prove that Alkaid offers deterministic robustness against bounded errors. To implement this scheme efficiently, we adopt block-wise and batch processing. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Alkaid achieves decoding success rates of 99\% to 100\% across diverse error channels, delivers a payload of 0.2 bits per token for high embedding capacity, and maintains an encoding speed of 6.72 bits per second, significantly surpassing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in robustness, capacity, and efficiency.

AI.tldr: Alkaid is a provably secure, edit-error-resilient steganographic scheme that uses distance-constrained encoding to ensure robustness, achieving high decoding success, capacity, and speed.
AI.motivation: Existing provably secure steganographic systems are vulnerable to edit errors (e.g., insertions, deletions, substitutions) due to reliance on perfect synchronization and lack of error correction, limiting their practicality in real-world applications.
AI.method: Alkaid uses distance-constrained encoding by integrating minimum distance decoding into the encoding process, enforcing a lower bound on edit distance between codewords; conflicting codewords are merged to ensure reliable recovery, with block-wise and batch processing for efficiency.
AI.result: Alkaid achieves 99% to 100% decoding success under various error channels, supports a payload of 0.2 bits per token, and operates at 6.72 bits per second, demonstrating superior robustness, capacity, and efficiency compared to current methods.
AI.conclusion: Alkaid represents a significant advancement in provably secure steganography by effectively combining theoretical security with practical robustness against real-world edit errors, outperforming SOTA methods in key performance metrics.

title: A Generalized Feature Model for Digital Twins
summary: The adoption of Digital Twin technologies is rapidly expanding in diverse industrial, economic, and societal domains. Over the past decade, a multitude of studies, surveys, and investigations have been conducted, examining the nature, applications, and advantages of Digital Twins. However, up until now, no proposal for a comprehensive feature model exists that effectively captures the mandatory and optional features of Digital Twins. To address this shortcoming, in this article, we present a general feature model for Digital Twins. Based on a systematic mapping study of existing literature, we developed a generalized feature model for Digital Models, Shadows, and Twins. To assess the validity of our proposed feature model, we have applied them to three use cases from the emergency, vehicular, and manufacturing domain. We conjecture that our proposed general feature model advances the field around Digital Twins by facilitating informed decision-making during design, enabling improved model-driven development of Digital Twins, and, eventually, fostering verification~\&~validation of Digital Twins by delivering a model-based foundation for test case inference.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a comprehensive feature model for Digital Twins derived from a systematic literature review, validated across emergency, vehicular, and manufacturing use cases, to support structured design, development, and validation of Digital Twins.
AI.motivation: Despite extensive research on Digital Twins, there is a lack of a comprehensive feature model that captures both mandatory and optional features, which hinders systematic design and development; this gap motivates the creation of a general feature model.
AI.method: A systematic mapping study of existing literature was conducted to develop a generalized feature model for Digital Models, Shadows, and Twins, which was then validated through application to three use cases from the emergency, vehicular, and manufacturing domains.
AI.result: A general feature model for Digital Twins was successfully developed and applied to three real-world use cases, demonstrating its applicability and validity across different domains.
AI.conclusion: The proposed general feature model advances the field of Digital Twins by supporting informed design decisions, enabling model-driven development, and facilitating verification and validation through a model-based foundation for test case inference.

title: SPOILER: TEE-Shielded DNN Partitioning of On-Device Secure Inference with Poison Learning
summary: Deploying deep neural networks (DNNs) on edge devices exposes valuable intellectual property to model-stealing attacks. While TEE-shielded DNN partitioning (TSDP) mitigates this by isolating sensitive computations, existing paradigms fail to simultaneously satisfy privacy and efficiency. The training-before-partition paradigm suffers from intrinsic privacy leakage, whereas the partition-before-training paradigm incurs severe latency due to structural dependencies that hinder parallel execution. To overcome these limitations, we propose SPOILER, a novel search-before-training framework that fundamentally decouples the TEE sub-network from the backbone via hardware-aware neural architecture search (NAS). SPOILER identifies a lightweight TEE architecture strictly optimized for hardware constraints, maximizing parallel efficiency. Furthermore, we introduce self-poisoning learning to enforce logical isolation, rendering the exposed backbone functionally incoherent without the TEE component. Extensive experiments on CNNs and Transformers demonstrate that SPOILER achieves state-of-the-art trade-offs between security, latency, and accuracy.

AI.tldr: SPOILER introduces a search-before-training framework for TEE-protected DNNs that uses hardware-aware NAS and self-poisoning to achieve strong security, low latency, and high accuracy on edge devices.
AI.motivation: Existing TEE-shielded DNN partitioning approaches face a trade-off between privacy and efficiency: training-before-partition leaks privacy, while partition-before-training incurs high latency due to limited parallelism.
AI.method: Proposes SPOILER, a search-before-training framework using hardware-aware neural architecture search (NAS) to decouple the TEE sub-network from the backbone, combined with self-poisoning learning to ensure functional incoherence of the exposed model component.
AI.result: SPOILER achieves state-of-the-art performance in balancing security, latency, and accuracy on CNNs and Transformers, with improved parallel efficiency and reduced privacy leakage.
AI.conclusion: SPOILER provides a secure, efficient, and accurate solution for DNN deployment on edge devices by decoupling TEE sub-networks via hardware-aware NAS and enforcing logical isolation through self-poisoning learning.

title: A Scalable Benchmark for Repository-Oriented Long-Horizon Conversational Context Management
summary: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, substantially enhancing their code understanding and generation capabilities and giving rise to powerful code assistants. However, in practical repository development, excessively long-horizon conversational context may overwhelm models, causing the loss of critical information and degraded performance, thereby limiting the utility of code assistants. Existing context management methods proposed to mitigate this context dilemma primarily target general-purpose conversations, while repository-oriented solutions remain largely unexplored, which is largely due to the lack of reliable evaluation benchmarks. To bridge this gap, we present LoCoEval, the first long-horizon conversational context management benchmark tailored to repository-oriented development scenarios. Adhering to three key principles, LoCoEval is constructed via an LLM-driven pipeline that generates realistic and diverse repository-oriented conversations, capturing key interaction patterns such as iterative requirements, noisy input, and retrospective questions. We evaluate 7 baselines, including 4 representative context management methods, using 3 advanced backbone LLMs on LoCoEval. The results reveal substantial challenges faced by standalone LLMs and existing approaches, especially memory systems, in repository-oriented conversational scenarios. To address these limitations, we further propose an improved method integrating conversational and repository information into a unified memory, which outperforms all baselines (*Oracle* excluded) and demonstrates robustness. Additionally, we investigated the impact of various factors on method performance, providing actionable insights for future research.

title: An Integrated Failure and Threat Mode and Effect Analysis (FTMEA) Framework with Quantified Cross-Domain Correlation Factors for Automotive Semiconductors
summary: The automotive industry faces increasing challenges in ensuring both functional safety (FuSa) and cybersecurity for complex semiconductor devices. Traditional Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) primarily addresses safety-related failure modes, often overlooking synergistic vulnerabilities and shared consequences with cybersecurity threats. This paper introduces an Integrated Failure and Threat Mode and Effect Analysis (FTMEA) framework that systematically co-analyzes FuSa and cybersecurity. A cornerstone of this framework is the introduction of rigorously defined Cross-Domain Correlation Factors (CDCFs), which quantify the interdependencies and mutual influences between safety-related failures and cybersecurity threats. These factors are derived from a combination of structured expert knowledge, static structural analysis metrics (e.g., Controllability/Observability), and validated against empirical data from fault/attack injection campaigns. We propose a modified Risk Priority Number (RPN) calculation that systematically integrates these correlation factors, enabling a more accurate and transparent prioritization of risks that span both domains. A detailed case study involving an automotive ASIC configuration register proves the practical application of the FTMEA. We present explicit mapping tables, quantitative CDCF values, and a comparative analysis against a baseline FMEA/TARA (Threat Analysis and Risk Assessment), illustrating how the integrated approach uncovers previously masked cross-domain risks, improves mitigation strategy effectiveness, and provides a clear quantitative justification for the derived correlation values. This framework offers a unified, traceable, methodology for risk assessment in critical automotive systems, thereby overcoming the limitations of conventional analyses and promoting optimized, cross-disciplinary development.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an Integrated Failure and Threat Mode and Effect Analysis (FTMEA) framework with Cross-Domain Correlation Factors (CDCFs) to jointly assess functional safety and cybersecurity in automotive semiconductors, enabling more accurate risk prioritization and revealing hidden cross-domain vulnerabilities.
AI.motivation: Traditional FMEA focuses on functional safety but neglects interactions with cybersecurity threats, leading to overlooked cross-domain risks in complex automotive semiconductor systems. There is a need for an integrated methodology that captures synergistic vulnerabilities and shared consequences between safety and security.
AI.method: The paper introduces an Integrated Failure and Threat Mode and Effect Analysis (FTMEA) framework with Cross-Domain Correlation Factors (CDCFs) derived from expert knowledge, structural metrics (e.g., Controllability/Observability), and empirical fault/attack injection data. It includes a modified Risk Priority Number (RPN) calculation that integrates CDCFs for cross-domain risk prioritization.
AI.result: The FTMEA framework successfully identifies previously masked cross-domain risks in an automotive ASIC case study. Quantitative CDCF values and mapping tables demonstrate improved risk prioritization and mitigation effectiveness compared to baseline FMEA/TARA, with empirical validation from fault and attack injection campaigns.
AI.conclusion: The proposed FTMEA framework with CDCFs enables a unified, traceable, and quantitative approach to co-analyze functional safety and cybersecurity in automotive semiconductors, overcoming the limitations of traditional isolated analyses and supporting optimized cross-disciplinary system development.

title: A Reference Architecture of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks
summary: The surge in reinforcement learning (RL) applications gave rise to diverse supporting technology, such as RL frameworks. However, the architectural patterns of these frameworks are inconsistent across implementations and there exists no reference architecture (RA) to form a common basis of comparison, evaluation, and integration. To address this gap, we propose an RA of RL frameworks. Through a grounded theory approach, we analyze 18 state-of-the-practice RL frameworks and, by that, we identify recurring architectural components and their relationships, and codify them in an RA. To demonstrate our RA, we reconstruct characteristic RL patterns. Finally, we identify architectural trends, e.g., commonly used components, and outline paths to improving RL frameworks.

AI.tldr: We propose a reference architecture (RA) for reinforcement learning (RL) frameworks based on a grounded theory analysis of 18 state-of-the-practice frameworks, identifying common components, relationships, and architectural trends to enable better comparison, evaluation, and integration.
AI.motivation: The lack of a standardized reference architecture for RL frameworks leads to inconsistent architectural patterns, hindering comparison, evaluation, and integration across different implementations.
AI.method: We applied a grounded theory approach to analyze 18 state-of-the-practice RL frameworks, identifying recurring architectural components and their relationships, which were then synthesized into a reference architecture.
AI.result: We developed a reference architecture for RL frameworks, reconstructed key RL design patterns using it, and identified common architectural trends such as frequently used components and integration practices.
AI.conclusion: The proposed reference architecture provides a common foundation for comparing, evaluating, and improving RL frameworks, promoting architectural consistency and advancing the state of the practice.

title: Designing Trustworthy Layered Attestations
summary:
Attestation means providing evidence that a remote target system is worthy of trust for some sensitive interaction. Although attestation is already used in network access control, security management, and trusted execution environments, it mainly concerns only a few system components. A clever adversary might manipulate these shallow attestations to mislead the relying party.
  Reliable attestations require layering. We construct attestations whose layers report evidence about successive components of the target system. Reliability also requires structuring the target system so only a limited set of components matters.
  We show how to structure an example system for reliable attestations despite a well-defined, relatively strong adversary. It is based on widely available hardware, such as Trusted Platform Modules, and software, such as Linux with SELinux. We isolate our principles in a few maxims that guide system development. We provide a cogent analysis of our mechanisms against our adversary model, as well as an empirical appraisal of the resulting system. We also identify two improvements to the mechanisms so attestation can succeed against strengthened adversaries. The performance burden of our attestation is negligible, circa 1.3 percent.
  After our first example, we vary our application level, and then also its underlying hardware anchor to use confidential computing with AMD's SEV-SNP. The same maxims help us achieve trustworthy attestations.

title: Understanding and Finding JIT Compiler Performance Bugs
summary: Just-in-time (JIT) compilers are key components for many popular programming languages with managed runtimes (e.g., Java and JavaScript). JIT compilers perform optimizations and generate native code at runtime based on dynamic profiling data, to improve the execution performance of the running application. Like other software systems, JIT compilers might have software bugs, and prior work has developed a number of automated techniques for detecting functional bugs (i.e., generated native code does not semantically match that of the original code). However, no prior work has targeted JIT compiler performance bugs, which can cause significant performance degradation while an application is running. These performance bugs are challenging to detect due to the complexity and dynamic nature of JIT compilers. In this paper, we present the first work on demystifying JIT performance bugs. First, we perform an empirical study across four popular JIT compilers for Java and JavaScript. Our manual analysis of 191 bug reports uncovers common triggers of performance bugs, patterns in which these bugs manifest, and their root causes. Second, informed by these insights, we propose layered differential performance testing, a lightweight technique to automatically detect JIT compiler performance bugs, and implement it in a tool called Jittery. We incorporate practical optimizations into Jittery such as test prioritization, which reduces testing time by 92.40% without compromising bug-detection capability, and automatic filtering of false-positives and duplicates, which substantially reduces manual inspection effort. Using Jittery, we discovered 12 previously unknown performance bugs in the Oracle HotSpot and Graal JIT compilers, with 11 confirmed and 6 fixed by developers.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic study of performance bugs in JIT compilers, identifying their characteristics through empirical analysis, and introduces Jittery, a tool using layered differential performance testing to effectively detect such bugs, resulting in 12 new bugs found in HotSpot and Graal, 11 confirmed and 6 fixed.
AI.motivation: While functional bugs in JIT compilers have been studied, performance bugs—those causing degradation without incorrect semantics—have been largely ignored despite their potential to severely impact runtime application performance. The motivation is to systematically understand, characterize, and effectively detect such performance bugs in JIT compilers.
AI.method: The authors conduct an empirical study on 191 bug reports from four popular JIT compilers (Java and JavaScript), identify root causes and patterns of performance bugs, and design a lightweight automated detection technique called layered differential performance testing. They implement this technique in a tool named Jittery, featuring test prioritization and false-positive/duplicate filtering, and evaluate it on Oracle HotSpot and Graal JIT compilers.
AI.result: The empirical study identifies common triggers, manifestation patterns, and root causes of JIT performance bugs. Jittery detects 12 previously unknown performance bugs in Oracle HotSpot and Graal, with 11 confirmed and 6 fixed by developers. Practical optimizations in Jittery reduce testing time by 92.40% and significantly cut down manual effort via automatic filtering.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that JIT performance bugs are a significant and previously understudied issue, and that layered differential performance testing, as implemented in Jittery, is an effective and efficient approach for uncovering such bugs in real-world JIT compilers.

title: Before You Hand Over the Wheel: Evaluating LLMs for Security Incident Analysis
summary:
Security incident analysis (SIA) poses a major challenge for security operations centers, which must manage overwhelming alert volumes, large and diverse data sources, complex toolchains, and limited analyst expertise. These difficulties intensify because incidents evolve dynamically and require multi-step, multifaceted reasoning. Although organizations are eager to adopt Large Language Models (LLMs) to support SIA, the absence of rigorous benchmarking creates significant risks for assessing their effectiveness and guiding design decisions. Benchmarking is further complicated by: (i) the lack of an LLM-ready dataset covering a wide spectrum of SIA tasks; (ii) the continual emergence of new tasks reflecting the diversity of analyst responsibilities; and (iii) the rapid release of new LLMs that must be incorporated into evaluations.
  In this paper, we address these challenges by introducing SIABENCH, an agentic evaluation framework for security incident analysis. First, we construct a first-of-its-kind dataset comprising two major SIA task categories: (i) deep analysis workflows for security incidents (25 scenarios) and (ii) alert-triage tasks (135 scenarios). Second, we implement an agent capable of autonomously performing a broad spectrum of SIA tasks (including network and memory forensics, malware analysis across binary/code/PDF formats, phishing email and kit analysis, log analysis, and false-alert detection). Third, we benchmark 11 major LLMs (spanning both open- and closed-weight models) on these tasks, with extensibility to support emerging models and newly added analysis scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SIABENCH, the first agentic evaluation framework for security incident analysis (SIA), featuring a novel dataset with 160 scenarios across deep analysis and alert-triage tasks, an autonomous agent for executing SIA tasks, and benchmarking of 11 major LLMs with support for future models and tasks.
AI.motivation: Security incident analysis is hindered by high alert volumes, heterogeneous data, complex workflows, and analyst shortages. While LLMs show promise, their adoption is impeded by the lack of standardized, comprehensive, and up-to-date benchmarking frameworks tailored to the dynamic nature of SIA.
AI.method: The authors design SIABENCH, which includes: (1) a dataset of 25 deep analysis and 135 alert-triage scenarios covering diverse SIA tasks; (2) an autonomous agent that simulates analyst behavior using tool integration and multi-step reasoning; and (3) a benchmarking pipeline to evaluate both open- and closed-weight LLMs across the full task spectrum, with modular support for new models and tasks.
AI.result: SIABENCH enables systematic evaluation of 11 state-of-the-art LLMs on realistic SIA workflows. The framework demonstrates strong coverage across critical domains including network forensics, malware analysis (binary/code/PDF), phishing detection, memory analysis, and false-alert identification, with measurable performance differences among models.
AI.conclusion: SIABENCH provides a rigorous, extensible foundation for evaluating LLMs in security incident analysis, addressing key gaps in dataset availability, task diversity, and model scalability, thereby advancing the responsible and effective integration of LLMs in real-world security operations.

title: Proteus: A Practical Framework for Privacy-Preserving Device Logs
summary: Device logs are essential for forensic investigations, enterprise monitoring, and fraud detection; however, they often leak personally identifiable information (PII) when exported for third-party analysis. Existing approaches either fail to minimize PII exposure across all stages of log collection and analysis or sacrifice data fidelity, resulting in less effective analysis. We present Proteus, a privacy-preserving device logging framework that enables forensic analysis without disclosing plaintext PII or compromising fidelity, even when facing adversaries with access to multiple snapshots of the log files. To achieve this, Proteus proposes a two-layer scheme that employs keyed-hash pseudonymization of PII fields and time-rotating encryption with ratcheted ephemeral keys to prevent multi-snapshot correlation. For controlled sharing, clients export ratchet states that grant time-bounded access, permitting decryption of pseudonymized tokens that enable linkage and timeline reconstruction without exposing the underlying PII. Subsequent ratchet rotations ensure forward secrecy, while DICE-based attestation authenticates device provenance. We implement Proteus as a transparent extension to Android's logcat and evaluate it across three generations of hardware. Our results demonstrate a median latency of 0.2 ms per message and an average per-PII-field size overhead of only 97.1 bytes.

AI.tldr: Proteus is a privacy-preserving logging framework that protects PII in device logs using pseudonymization and time-ratcheted encryption, enabling secure forensic analysis with minimal overhead and strong adversarial resistance.
AI.motivation: Device logs are valuable for forensics and monitoring but often leak PII when shared externally; existing methods either expose sensitive data or degrade analysis quality, creating a need for a system that preserves both privacy and data fidelity.
AI.method: Proteus uses a two-layer privacy scheme: (1) keyed-hash pseudonymization of PII fields and (2) time-rotating encryption with ratcheted ephemeral keys for forward secrecy. It enables controlled sharing via exported ratchet states for time-bounded decryption, and integrates DICE-based attestation for device authentication. Implemented as an extension to Android's logcat.
AI.result: Proteus achieves median latency of 0.2 ms per log message and adds only 97.1 bytes overhead per PII field. It resists correlation attacks across log snapshots, enables timeline reconstruction without exposing PII, and supports authenticated device provenance via DICE.
AI.conclusion: Proteus provides a practical and secure solution for privacy-preserving device logging, enabling forensic analysis with minimal PII exposure, strong resistance against multi-snapshot adversaries, and negligible performance overhead.
